items.q: A 68-year-old man has sudden left leg pallor with severe pain and no pulses for six hours. He can wriggle toes with intact sensation. Which Rutherford logic best classes this sensory-intact motion-preserved sudden ischaemia as salvageable?
o: Viable limbs sensing and moving suit urgent revascularisation
items.exp:
**Answer: A - Viable limbs sensing and moving suit urgent revascularisation.** Intact nerves with movement mark Rutherford viable limbs where minutes save muscle.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Dead limbs lose sense
- C: Motion proves viability
- D: Pallor varies with time
**Key point:** Sensory-intact sudden ischaemia revascularises urgently.
items.kp: Sensory-intact acute ischaemia is Rutherford salvageable.

items.q: A 74-year-old woman has atrial fibrillation with sudden right leg ischaemia and no prior claudication. Her arteries feel soft without bruits. Which embolic logic best blames fresh heart clots in sudden ischaemia without arterial disease?

items.exp:
**Answer: A - Clean arteries with fibrillating hearts embolise suddenly.** Unscarred vessels with quivering atria receive travelling clots without warning.
**Why the others are wrong**
- B: Soft vessels receive emboli
- C: Fibrillation breeds clots
- D: Emboli strike without warning
**Key point:** Sudden ischaemia in clean arteries means embolus.
items.kp: Sudden ischaemia without disease means cardiac embolus.

items.q: A 62-year-old man has ten-day calf claudication turned sudden pallor with a thrombosed popliteal aneurysm. His history spans years of aches. Which thrombotic logic best separates diseased-artery thrombosis from sudden emboli?

items.exp:

- D: Diseased beds clot

items.kp: Claudication history marks in-situ thrombosis over embolus.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman has heparin started the moment acute ischaemia is diagnosed, before imaging completes. The team explains clot propagation halts. Which heparin-first logic best starts anticoagulation at diagnosis before plans finalise?
